For multi-step agent applications, the same traces that power debugging feed the trajectory-level judges, and callback-based integrations (LangChain, LlamaIndex — see /llama-index/ for context on that ecosystem) mean agent frameworks can log without code changes. Provider coverage is broad: track_openai at L24 monkey-patches the OpenAI client via OpenaiChatCompletionsTrackDecorator, L32, and the integrations/ package ships similar trackers for Anthropic, Gemini, LiteLLM, Bedrock, and more.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you bet a project on this:

  • The SDK is one piece of a three-piece system. sdks/python is only the client; the backend lives under apps/ in the same monorepo, and deployment/ carries the docker-compose stack for self-hosting. Reading the SDK alone tells you nothing about backend scaling characteristics — evaluate the whole stack if you plan to self-host.
  • LLM judges are opinionated prompts, not ground truth. The hallucination and factuality judges ship fixed templates; their scores are only as good as the judge model you point them at, and the docs themselves steer you toward reviewing results rather than trusting them blindly. For benchmark-grade measurement, deterministic metrics or an external harness remain the safer instrument.
  • The REST client is generated. The rest_api/ package is Fern-generated — thousands of mechanical lines. That is good for correctness and bad for grep-driven reading; the hand-written logic you want to study lives in api_objects/ and message_processing/.
  • Async support has caveats. The decorator handles sync and async functions, and an AsyncOpikApi exists at L212, but the message queue is threaded rather than asyncio-native; extremely high-concurrency asyncio services should measure the queue’s behavior under load before committing.
  • Benchmarks are yours to run. The repo publishes no latency or overhead numbers for the tracing hot path. The design (fire-and-forget put(), background batching) is sound, but trust your own measurement on your own traffic.

Overall, Opik is one of the more thoughtfully layered SDKs in the LLM-tooling space: a clean facade, a genuinely decoupled write path, and an evaluation layer that grew real depth without losing its toy-like ease of use. If observability is the problem you are shopping for, it belongs on a shortlist of two or three — and the source is readable enough that the shortlisting can start with a quiet afternoon in sdks/python.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of the Opik Python SDK: tracing, datasets, experiments, evaluation metrics, and the batching machinery that keeps telemetry off the hot path.

entry.title: Arize Phoenix Source Tour: Inside the Open-Source OTel-Native LLM Tracing Server

link.title: Arize Phoenix Source Tour: Inside the Open-Source OTel-Native LLM Tracing Server

entry.content:
If you have ever shipped an LLM application and then asked “what did the model actually see, and what did it answer?”, you already understand the problem Arize set out to solve with Phoenix. Phoenix is an open-source, OpenTelemetry-native observability platform for LLM apps: it ingests traces and spans from your agents, RAG systems, and SDK calls, stores them in a real database, and gives you a web UI plus REST and GraphQL APIs to query, annotate, and evaluate them. It also does evals — LLM-graded scoring of outputs like retrieval relevance, hallucination, and question-answering correctness.

What makes Phoenix interesting to read at the source level is that it is not a toy collector. The main package boots a FastAPI application with a Strawberry GraphQL schema, an async gRPC server implementing the standard OpenTelemetry trace service, a background bulk-insert writer, and a SQLAlchemy storage layer that runs on SQLite by default with PostgreSQL as the scale-out option. Everything speaks OTLP, so any OpenTelemetry-instrumented program can ship traces to it without vendor lock-in.

This post is a source tour of the Arize-ai/phoenix repository at its main branch. Phoenix is a monorepo: the core server lives under src/phoenix/, and three lightweight Python sub-packages — arize-phoenix-otel, arize-phoenix-client, and arize-phoenix-evals — live under packages/. I verified every file path, symbol name, and line number below against the checked-out tree, and mapped the whole system into two diagrams. The first shows the shape of the system; the second goes one level deeper into each area.

Overview of Phoenix at `main`: the arize-phoenix-otel package exports spans to either the gRPC or HTTP ingest surface of the server; a bulk inserter writes them into SQLAlchemy-backed storage; REST, GraphQL, and notebook sessions read the same rows; and the client and evals packages talk back over the versioned REST API.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • register(), L65 — the entry point of arize-phoenix-otel. It wraps OpenTelemetry primitives with Phoenix-aware defaults (endpoint, project name, headers) and auto-instruments any installed OpenInference libraries so LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI, and friends start emitting spans with no extra code.
  • run(), L217 — what phoenix serve actually executes. It reads every environment variable up front, builds the async database session factory, and hands the app to uvicorn.
  • create_app(), L939 — the FastAPI factory that assembles middleware, the v1 REST router, the GraphQL router, the gRPC server, and the bulk inserter in one place. If you only read one file in the repo, read this one.
  • Export(), L41 — the gRPC handler implementing the OpenTelemetry TraceService. It walks resource_spans, resolves the project name from resource attributes, and enqueues each decoded span.
  • post_traces(), L461 — the HTTP/JSON twin of the gRPC path, mounted at POST /v1/traces and advertised in the boot banner as otlp_http_url.
  • decode_otlp_span(), L97 — converts protobuf OTLP spans into Phoenix’s own Span dataclasses, synthesizing OpenInference attributes along the way.
  • BulkInserter, L115 — the background writer that batches queued spans and annotations, retries transient failures, and flushes them to the database.
  • Span, L867 — the SQLAlchemy ORM model at the bottom of the stack, next to Trace (L808), Project (L740), Dataset (L1438), and Experiment (L1680).

The detail view: instrumentation internals on the left, the server entry chain and OTLP ingest in the middle, the write path into the ORM models, and the three query/read surfaces plus the client and evals packages on the right.

The Write Path: From SDK Call to Database Row

The ingest story is the heart of Phoenix. On the instrumentation side, register() returns a Phoenix-flavored TracerProvider (L200) that wires up either an HTTPSpanExporter (L541) or a GRPCSpanExporter (L619), depending on the endpoint scheme you configured. That means the same register() call works whether your Phoenix is local, containerized, or remote.

On the server side, GrpcServer (L55) owns the grpc.aio server lifecycle — port binding, optional TLS and mutual TLS, and interceptors, including an API-key interceptor when authentication is enabled. Its Servicer.Export runs the protobuf-to-domain translation in a thread pool (so the event loop never blocks on decoding) and then hands each (span, project_name) pair to an async enqueue callback.

Everything lands in the BulkInserter. Rather than writing each span as it arrives, Phoenix queues them and lets _insert_spans() (L283) drain the queue in batches, calling insert_span() (L128) to persist rows inside a session. After each successful insert, DML events flow into DmlEventHandler (L243), which fans them out to GraphQL subscriptions and cache invalidation — that is how a live UI shows new traces without polling.

Two practical details worth knowing: the HTTP ingest endpoint and the gRPC endpoint accept the same OTLP payloads (one in JSON form, one in protobuf form), so you can point the OpenTelemetry collector, arize-phoenix-otel, or any OTLP-capable SDK at either. And spans carry OpenInference semantic-convention attributes — prompt text, completion text, retrieval documents, token counts — which is what makes the UI render actual model conversations instead of raw key-value noise.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a working Phoenix plus a traced application is a five-minute job. The steps below come straight from the repository README and the verified code paths above.

First, install and boot the server. The README quickstart is two lines, with a no-install alternative via uvx:

pip install arize-phoenix
phoenix serve
# or: uvx arize-phoenix serve

The server listens on port 6006 by default (the client’s documented fallback is http://localhost:6006), prints a boot banner listing its UI, REST, GraphQL, and OTLP endpoints, and creates a SQLite database on first run. run() in the serve command resolves all of this from environment variables, and create_app() applies migrations on boot through the engine factory.

Second, wire up tracing. The fastest path is the coding-agent setup command from the README (npx @arizeai/phoenix-cli setup, or px setup with Phoenix installed), which detects your framework and LLM provider and installs the matching OpenInference instrumentation. If you prefer code, install the small OTel wrapper package:

from phoenix.otel import register

tracer_provider = register()  # auto-instruments installed OpenInference libraries

That single call returns a configured TracerProvider and starts exporting spans to your local server. If you use LangChain or LlamaIndex, the instrumentation hooks emit ready-made traces with prompts, retrievals, and token usage — see our LangChain and LlamaIndex source tours for how those frameworks’ internals look from the outside.

Third, query and export what you collected. Install the client package (pip install arize-phoenix-client) and use the typed REST client:

from phoenix.client import Client

client = Client()  # defaults to http://localhost:6006
df = client.spans.get_spans_dataframe()   # export trace data as pandas
client.datasets.create_dataset(...)       # version prompts and examples

Client (L20 of the client module) exposes resource objects for prompts, projects, spans, traces, sessions, datasets, and experiments, each mapping onto the v1 REST surface. The classic notebook experience still works too: import phoenix as px and call launch_app() (L268), which starts or attaches to a server and returns a Session object for in-notebook browsing.

Datasets, Experiments, and Evals

Phoenix treats evaluation as a first-class workflow rather than an afterthought. A Dataset is versioned: examples you upload (individually via the client’s create_dataset and add_examples_to_dataset, or as CSV/JSONL uploads) are frozen into versions so an experiment’s results always reference the exact inputs used. An Experiment then records the outputs of a task function run over those examples, along with evaluator scores — the client’s Experiments resource (L592 of its module) orchestrates the run and accepts evaluator callables.

The arize-phoenix-evals package supplies the graders. Evaluator (L305) is the abstract base, LLMEvaluator (L515) wraps any LLM with a prompt template to score outputs (relevance, hallucination, QA correctness), and ClassificationEvaluator (L607) maps raw model responses onto labeled choices. Scores land back in Phoenix as span or trace annotations, which is how the UI renders per-row eval badges. If you have used OpenAI’s evals harness, the mental model is similar — see our openai-evals tour for the comparison point — but Phoenix binds the results to specific traces, so a bad score is one click away from the conversation that caused it.

The Query Surfaces

One database, three read paths. The v1 REST router (create_v1_router (L35)) is the stable, versioned surface the Python and TypeScript clients target, with cursor-paginated endpoints like list_project_traces (L148). The GraphQL schema (build_graphql_schema (L67), mounted via create_graphql_router (L801)) is what the React UI actually consumes, including subscriptions fed by the DML event handler. And the notebook Session classes offer an embedded experience where a Phoenix server runs in a background thread or process next to your kernel.

It is worth appreciating the consistency here: all three surfaces read the same SQLAlchemy models, and all writes — OTLP ingest, annotations logged via REST, dataset uploads — flow through the same bulk-inserter write path. That single-writer design is what keeps the SQLite default viable for individual use.

Honest Limits

A few caveats, all checkable in the repository:

  • Storage scale. The default engine is SQLite, with PostgreSQL supported for multi-user deployments (both engine factories live in src/phoenix/db/engines.py). The repo ships Docker Compose, Helm charts, and cloud deployment templates for the Postgres path. There is no distributed collector story in-process: it is one server, optionally fronted by an OTel collector.
  • The UI is out of scope here. The React frontend lives in js/app (TypeScript) and is a substantial codebase on its own; this tour covered the Python side that serves it.
  • Package churn. Phoenix has evolved quickly — MIGRATION.md at the repo root documents breaking changes, and older tutorials using px.Client() predate the newer phoenix.client.Client. Parts of phoenix-evals carry deprecation warnings as templating APIs are consolidated. Pin versions and check the changelog before upgrading.
  • Evals are LLM-graded, not ground truth. The eval package’s scores come from whatever model you give it; treat them as measurements that need their own spot-checking, not as verdicts.
  • Self-hosting vs cloud. Everything described here runs locally and for free under the project’s license, but Phoenix (the product) also has a hosted cloud offering with additional features — the open-source repo is the self-hosted core.

For context on the wider landscape, Langfuse and Opik are the two other open-source LLM observability servers we have toured; Phoenix’s distinguishing bet is full OpenTelemetry alignment end to end — the same protobuf OTLP service your APM already speaks, applied to LLM traces.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Arize Phoenix, the open-source OpenTelemetry-native tracing and evaluation server for LLM applications.

entry.title: Pydantic source tour: how BaseModel turns type hints into validators and serializers

link.title: Pydantic source tour: how BaseModel turns type hints into validators and serializers

entry.content:
Pydantic is the quiet dependency under a remarkable amount of the modern Python stack. If you have ever declared a FastAPI endpoint, asked an LLM for structured output with instructor, defined tools with the MCP Python SDK, or let an agent framework check its own inputs, a pydantic model did the actual checking. The project describes itself plainly in the README: “Data validation using Python type hints,” fast and extensible, where you “define how data should be in pure, canonical Python 3.10+; validate it with Pydantic.” That one-sentence promise hides an intricate machine, and this post opens the hood.

What makes the repository interesting is the split of responsibilities. The Python package you import (pydantic) is an orchestration layer: it watches your class definitions, collects your annotations and decorators, and compiles everything into an internal description called a core schema. The actual validation and serialization loops run in the Rust-powered pydantic-core crate that the package depends on. So reading the Python side is really about understanding one thing deeply: how a class body like id: int plus a decorator or two becomes a compiled validator that rejects bad data and a serializer that emits clean output. This tour walks that path through the current main branch, where pydantic/version.py reports version 2.15.0a0+dev at the time of writing.

We prepared two architecture diagrams from the tree. The overview shows the four neighborhoods of the codebase and how your code reaches them; the detail diagram goes one level deeper into the specific functions that do the work. Every node links back to the real source on GitHub, so you can click through while reading. Line numbers below were verified against main at the time of the tour.

Overview of pydantic's architecture: your application imports the public surface, the metaclass builds each model from config, fields and decorators, and the schema engine turns it all into compiled validators plus JSON Schema.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BaseModel, L136 in pydantic/main.py is the class you actually subclass. It also hosts the runtime API you call every day: model_validate, L749, model_dump, L472, and model_dump_json, L538.
  • ModelMetaclass, L88 in _model_construction.py is the hook that runs the moment Python executes your class User(BaseModel): statement. Nothing about a model is ready before this metaclass finishes.
  • ConfigWrapper, L62 in _internal/_config.py takes your model_config = ConfigDict(...) and resolves it against inherited settings into one checked object.
  • FieldInfo, L99 in fields.py is the metadata object behind every field; the Field, L1327 function is how you tune it inline in a class body.
  • GenerateSchema, L356 in _internal/_generate_schema.py is the heart of the machine: it converts type hints, fields and decorator functions into a core schema.
  • DecoratorInfos, L414 in _internal/_decorators.py is the registry where your field_validator, model_validator and serializer declarations are collected before schema building.
  • GenerateJsonSchema, L223 in json_schema.py projects all of that structure outward as standard JSON Schema documents.
  • MockValSer, L76 in _internal/_mock_val_ser.py covers the awkward case where a model cannot be finished yet — say, a forward reference that is still undefined — by installing placeholders that attempt a rebuild on first use.

The detailed view groups pydantic into six layers: the public API surface, model construction internals, core schema generation, the validation layer built from decorators, the serialization layer, and the JSON Schema bridge.

From Install to Your First Model

Start with the README’s instruction: pip install -U pydantic (or conda install pydantic -c conda-forge). No compiled Python-side dependencies beyond the pydantic-core binary wheel are needed, which is why installation is usually uneventful even on exotic platforms.

Then define a model exactly the way the README does:

from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str = 'John Doe'
    signup_ts: Optional[datetime] = None
    friends: list[int] = []

external_data = {'id': '123', 'signup_ts': '2017-06-01 12:22', 'friends': [1, '2', b'3']}
user = User(**external_data)
print(user.id)
#> 123

Three things happened in that snippet. First, the four annotated attributes were collected into FieldInfo objects, with defaults preserved and id marked required because it has no default. Second, the string '123' was coerced to the integer 123, and messy list items like '2' and b'3' became clean ints — that is the lenient “smart” mode, and User.model_validate(external_data) exercises the identical generated validator; the classmethod is defined at model_validate, L749 and simply delegates to cls.__pydantic_validator__.validate_python(...), the compiled validator attached to your class. Third, model_dump() returns a plain dictionary and model_dump_json() returns a JSON string, both with knobs for include/exclude, aliases, exclude_unset, and a mode switch between Python-native and JSON-ready output.

The outbound side mirrors the inbound side. For schema documentation, User.model_json_schema() — the convenience function at model_json_schema, L2734 — hands you a standards-shaped JSON Schema for the model, which is precisely what tools like FastAPI and the MCP Python SDK embed in their generated interfaces.

Class Creation: What Happens Before __init__ Runs

The metaclass is where pydantic departs from ordinary Python. When ModelMetaclass.__new__ executes, it walks the new class in a fixed order. set_model_fields, L528 converts the annotations into the field map; ConfigWrapper, L62 merges the model’s model_config with everything inherited from parent classes; and the decorator registry DecoratorInfos, L414 gathers every validation and serialization decorator you declared. Only then does complete_model_class, L561 call the schema engine, attach the resulting compiled validator and serializer to __pydantic_validator__ and __pydantic_serializer__, and your class is open for business.

If any annotation cannot be resolved yet — a forward reference to a class defined later, a type imported lazily — pydantic does not fail at import time. It installs the MockValSer, L76 placeholders, which raise a helpful error if touched and attempt to rebuild the real validator once the missing pieces exist. That is why pydantic models can be spread across modules that reference each other in loops, a situation ordinary dataclass-based designs handle poorly.

The Schema Engine: One Visitor for Every Type

GenerateSchema, L356 is the largest and most important internal class. Its entry method generate_schema, L794 caches results per type, then _generate_schema_inner, L1099 dispatches on the annotation’s shape: primitives, generics, literals, unions, dataclasses, or models. For model classes it builds a nested schema via _model_schema, L839, reading each FieldInfo and the resolved config, and wiring in the standard validators it reuses from _internal/_validators.py, such as sequence_validator, L28 for lists, sets and tuples.

The elegant part is that everything in the ecosystem funnels through this one engine. TypeAdapter, L69 lets you validate a bare type like list[Task] without inventing a wrapper model, and it calls the same generate_schema machinery. Standard-library dataclasses get the treatment through complete_dataclass, L85, and even plain function signatures can be validated at runtime with validate_call, L83. One visitor, many surfaces — which is why behavior stays consistent whether you entered through a model, an adapter, a dataclass, or a decorated function.

Validators, Serializers, and the JSON Schema Bridge

Custom logic enters through a small set of decorators, and each one is pure bookkeeping until the schema engine consumes it. The field_validator, L410 decorator registers a per-field check by producing a FieldValidatorDecoratorInfo, L55 record; the model_validator, L677 decorator does the same for whole-object checks via ModelValidatorDecoratorInfo, L134. On the way out, field_serializer, L224 and model_serializer, L355 attach custom dumping behavior, recorded as FieldSerializerDecoratorInfo, L92. For inline use inside Annotated, PlainSerializer, L21 and WrapSerializer, L91 wrap a function so it travels with the type annotation itself rather than with a specific class.

Once the core schema exists, the JSON Schema side is a read-only projection. GenerateJsonSchema, L223 walks the core schema and emits the standard document, and because it is a class you can subclass, teams customize titles, descriptions, or OpenAPI-flavored output without touching validation. Edge shapes are supported too: RootModel, L34 wraps a bare root value when the whole payload is, say, a list rather than an object.

This composability is exactly why the library has become the lingua franca for structured data in the LLM world. instructor leans on pydantic models to turn free-form chat completions into typed objects, and the validation errors loop straight back into the prompt as repair feedback. The pydantic team’s own pydantic-ai framework uses the same models to type agent tools and results, and the MCP Python SDK describes tool inputs and outputs with them as well. Learn one model syntax here and you have learned the interface all three expect.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you build on this tour:

  • The Python layer is not where the speed lives. The validation and serialization hot loops run inside the Rust pydantic-core crate, which this tour deliberately did not open. The Python package’s job — metaclass orchestration, schema building, decorator bookkeeping — happens once per class definition, not per instance.
  • No benchmark numbers here on purpose. The README advertises pydantic as “Fast” without publishing figures in that document, and we did not run our own measurements, so this post makes no performance claims.
  • V2 is a different library from V1. The README states plainly that Pydantic V2 is “a ground-up rewrite” with breaking changes. The repository ships an in-tree V1 compatibility copy under pydantic/v1/ (usable as from pydantic import v1 as pydantic_v1), and deprecated helpers such as parse_obj_as, L31 still live in pydantic/deprecated/. Settings management, formerly BaseSettings, moved to the separate pydantic-settings package; the in-repo pydantic/env_settings.py is explicitly a “backport module from V1” per its own docstring.
  • Line numbers drift. We toured main at version 2.15.0a0+dev. Every file and line cited here was verified with search at writing time, but main moves; the diagrams and their click-through links reflect the branch as of this post’s date.
  • Schema building has a real cost. The metaclass work is per-class, but huge models, deeply nested unions, and heavy decorator use all widen the schema-building step; deferred builds via the mock placeholders exist precisely because some classes cannot be completed eagerly.

If you want to go deeper into the ecosystem after this tour, the structured-output workflow in instructor is the natural next stop, and the agent-side patterns in pydantic-ai show the same models driving tool-calling loops end to end.

entry.title: Ray Source Tour: How Tasks, Actors and the Object Store Fit Together

link.title: Ray Source Tour: How Tasks, Actors and the Object Store Fit Together

entry.content:
Ray began as a research project at UC Berkeley and grew into what its README now calls “a unified framework for scaling AI and Python applications.” The pitch is simple: the same Python you run on your laptop should run on a cluster with minimal changes. What makes that work is a surprisingly compact core — a driver library that decorates your functions and classes, a set of per-node processes that schedule and execute work, and a distributed object store that moves the results around. In this tour we read the actual Python source of ray-project/ray (the python/ray package on the master branch) and trace a call from ray.init() down to the C++ core worker and back.

The two diagrams below were generated from the repository itself: every node links to a real file on GitHub, and every symbol we mention is one we located with a line-number search in the working tree. The first diagram is a map of the whole system — the public API, the cluster bootstrap machinery, the task and actor paths, and the object layer. The second goes deeper into internals: function export and registration, actor creation, and how ray.put and ray.get interact with the core worker. If you have read our earlier tours of single-machine tools like Dask, this is the natural next step: Ray’s design decisions only become visible at cluster scale.

Ray overview — twelve files that define the system's shape. Click any node to open the source on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • ray.init at L1448 in _private/worker.py is the front door. It either attaches to an existing cluster or builds a local one, and the module-level global_worker = Worker() at L1408 means every process has exactly one worker instance.
  • Node at L73 in _private/node.py describes one machine’s configuration, and ray.init constructs it at L1930 for the head-node case.
  • The process launcher in _private/services.py — start_ray_process at L883, with dedicated helpers like start_gcs_server at L1523 and start_raylet at L1610 — actually forks the GCS, raylet, and dashboard processes you see in ps output.
  • ray.remote at L3804 is the decorator entry point. Its helper _make_remote at L3611 checks whether you decorated a function or a class and routes accordingly.
  • RemoteFunction at L41 in remote_function.py is the stateless-task wrapper. Setting self.remote = _remote_proxy at L183 is what gives your function its .remote() method, and calling the wrapper directly raises TypeError at L185.
  • ActorClass at L1553 is the stateful counterpart, and the ActorHandle at L2274 it returns is the proxy your code holds for the actor’s lifetime.
  • ObjectRef at L50 is a Cython class (cdef class ObjectRef(BaseID)) that wraps an object ID plus owner address — it is the future-like handle every task and method call returns.
  • SerializationContext at L145 registers the custom deserializers that make refs and actor handles cross process boundaries intact.
  • Above the core sit the libraries: Tuner at L43 for hyperparameter search and Dataset at L272 for data-parallel loading and transformation. Both are ordinary consumers of the task and actor APIs you see beneath them.

The Task Path: From Decorator to Worker

Follow the task path in the detail diagram. When you write @ray.remote on a function, _make_remote wraps it in a RemoteFunction whose options were validated at decoration time. Nothing runs yet. The first call of f.remote(...) lands in RemoteFunction._remote at L358, and this is where three important things happen.

First, the function is exported. Because the receiving worker is a different process that has never seen your code, Ray pickles the function and ships it through the FunctionActorManager.export at L219 method of function_manager.py. There is an export-once guard: _last_export_cluster_and_job is compared against the worker’s current cluster and job, so the pickle round-trip happens once per function per job rather than on every call. On the execution side, a worker that picks up the task calls fetch_and_register_remote_function at L289 to pull the pickled blob from the cluster’s key-value store and re-import it locally.

Second, arguments are flattened and serialized against the extracted function signature, using the machinery in SerializationContext. If an argument is itself an ObjectRef, Ray passes it by reference and the receiving worker resolves it; only plain values are inlined into the task spec.

Third, the prepared task is handed to the C++ side. The Python driver’s worker.core_worker is a ray._raylet.CoreWorker binding created at L2735 inside connect(). That single binding is the wall between the readable Python layer and the scheduling, ownership, and object-store logic implemented in C++ under src/ray (outside the Python package we toured here). The call returns immediately with an ObjectRef — Ray’s task submission is asynchronous by design, and your script only blocks when it asks for a result.

The Actor Path: Stateful Workers

Actors answer a different question: what if a worker should keep state between calls? ActorClass at L1553 is what @ray.remote produces for a class. Its metaclass-style __init__ at L1562 exists mostly to forbid subclassing an actor class directly, and __call__ raises if you try to instantiate it like a normal Python object — the only legal entry point is .remote().

That call goes to ActorClass._remote at L1883. It validates naming and namespace options, exports the class definition through export_actor_class at L488 in the same manager the task path uses, computes the actor’s resource footprint, and finally invokes core_worker.create_actor at L2193. The result is wrapped into an ActorHandle at L2274 — note the original_handle=True argument at creation, which matters for ownership: when the original handle goes out of scope, the actor itself can be destroyed.

Method calls are the elegant part. ActorHandle defines a __getattr__ at L2610 that returns an ActorMethod (the class lives at L848) for any attribute you touch. Calling it lands in _actor_method_call at L2486, which serializes the arguments and reaches core_worker.submit_actor_task at L2578. The return value is again one or more ObjectRefs. Concurrency semantics depend on configuration: an async actor runs tasks on an event loop, while threaded actors default to out-of-order execution — the code around L2167 shows allow_out_of_order_execution being defaulted from is_asyncio or max_concurrency > 1.

For coordination across a fixed set of actors, the standard library utility is ActorPool at L13 in util/actor_pool.py, which distributes work items over your handles and yields results as they complete. It is a small file and one of the best places to see actor handles being used the way Ray’s own authors intended.

Objects: ObjectRef, ray.put and ray.get

The object layer is the third pillar. ray.put at L3053 stores a value once and hands you a ref you can pass to any task; Worker.put_object at L810 does the work, retrying automatically when the store is full. ray.get at L2902 blocks until the value is available locally — if it lives on another node, the system ships it over first — and it will re-raise a task’s exception in your process, which is why errors from remote code look local. ray.wait at L3109 splits a list of refs into ready and not-ready without blocking on all of them, and is the standard tool for bounding how many tasks are in flight.

The ObjectRef itself, defined in Cython at includes/object_ref.pxi L50, is more than a token: it registers itself with the core worker on construction and deregisters on deallocation (L68 and the __dealloc__ that follows), which is how Ray’s distributed reference counting knows when a value can be evicted. It also supports await via as_future, so the same ref works in asyncio code. Inside a worker, get_runtime_context at L641 in runtime_context.py exposes the current job, task, and actor IDs so library code can introspect where it is running. One more detail worth knowing: in __init__.py, AUTO_INIT_APIS at L207 lists the public functions (get, put, wait, cancel, and friends) that implicitly call ray.init() for you — remote deliberately is not in that set, because decorating should never start a cluster.

Ray internals — the task path from decorator to core worker, the actor path with handles and method calls, and the object layer they both share.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above is verifiable from the quick-start path in the README and the remote() docstring, which contains the exact example we adapt here.

Step 1 — install:

pip install ray

Step 2 — turn a plain function into a remote task with the decorator:

import ray
ray.init()

@ray.remote
def train_chunk(seed: int):
    # pretend this trains a small model and returns its score
    total = sum(i * i for i in range(seed * 1_000))
    return seed, total

Step 3 — submit all chunks at once and collect with ray.get. The calls return immediately; the loop only blocks at the single ray.get:

refs = [train_chunk.remote(s) for s in range(8)]
results = ray.get(refs)          # blocks until all eight finish
print(results[:2])

Step 4 — make it stateful. A model server is naturally an actor, and the docstring for ray.remote shows the class form verbatim:

@ray.remote
class Scorer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = 0
    def score(self, x):
        self.calls += 1
        return x * 2

scorer = Scorer.remote()
ref = scorer.score.remote(21)
print(ray.get(ref))              # 42

Step 5 — scale out. The same script runs unchanged on a real cluster: start nodes with ray start --head / ray start --address=<head> and point ray.init(address=...) at the cluster. That is the whole migration story, and it is the reason the core API surface is so small — tasks, actors, and objects cover what the AI libraries need.

Where the Libraries Plug In

The overview diagram’s right edge shows two representative consumers. Ray Tune’s Tuner expresses hyperparameter search as many parallel trials, each an actor or task, and borrows the scheduling and fault-tolerance of the core rather than reimplementing it. Ray Data’s Dataset decomposes a large dataset into blocks and processes them with streaming tasks, which is the same task/actor substrate again. This layering is why Ray’s README lists its AI libraries — Data, Train, Tune, RLlib, Serve — as separate products while the runtime underneath stays shared. If you are comparing distributed-dataframe options, our Modin tour (here) covers a library that can use Ray as an execution engine, and our Dask tour (here) covers its closest architectural cousin in task-graph land.

Honest Limits

Three limitations deserve plain language. First, the C++ heart is out of scope here: scheduling policy, the ownership model described in the “Ownership” paper referenced in the README, and the Plasma-derived object store live in src/ray, so this tour stops at the CoreWorker binding — the diagrams describe the Python side truthfully, but the most interesting scheduling code is on the far side of that wall. Second, the Python package is enormous (over ten thousand files in the sparse checkout we searched), and much of its bulk is tests, autoscaler cloud providers, and protocol-generated code; the handful of files we anchor on are the ones the public API actually routes through. Third, we deliberately quote no performance numbers in this post: any claim about throughput or latency would need a benchmark we did not run, and the README itself makes no such claims. What we can say is structural — Ray trades a small, stable API for a large amount of process machinery, and reading the source makes that trade visible: ray.init starts real operating-system processes, decoration creates real wrappers with real validation, and every .remote() call crosses a language boundary. Understanding those costs is exactly what a source tour is for. For inference-scale serving built on similar distributed runtimes, see our vLLM (tour) and SGLang (tour).
entry.summary: A guided architecture tour of the ray-project/ray Python package, from ray.init to ActorHandle and ObjectRef, with clickable diagrams.
